title: Contextual Facilitation Without Prediction-Error Cost in Chinese Reading: Eye-Tracking Evidence for Graded Pre-Activation
content: Within the framework of predictive coding, language comprehension is conceptualized as a process of probabilistic inference, wherein comprehenders leverage contextual priors to anticipate upcoming input. However, the extent to which this process is modulated by extralinguistic factors-specifically emotional valence and individual differences in empathy remains a subject of debate. Using eye-tracking, the present study examined the interplay of contextual constraint, target predictability, and verb valence in Chinese sentence reading, with trait empathy modeled as a key moderator. The results demonstrated a robust contextual predictability effect driven predominantly by facilitation, with a notable absence of canonical prediction-error costs for unpredictable words in high-constraint contexts. This pattern lends support to graded pre-activation accounts over rigid lexical prediction mechanisms. Crucially, the findings reveal that emotional valence and empathy modulate reading dynamics via functionally dissociable mechanisms. Emotional valence primarily regulated information-sampling heuristics rather than altering the speed of lexical access per se. In contrast, exploratory analyses suggested that trait empathy may be associated with differences in later eye-movement patterns: high-empathy individuals showed reduced skipping and longer late-stage processing under high uncertainty, whereas low-empathy individuals showed delayed processing costs during late integration. These findings suggest that predictive processing in Chinese is supported by probabilistic semantic constraints and is not a monolithic mechanism, but rather is dynamically shaped by the reader’s socio-cognitive profile and the affective properties of the context.
